metadata.title: Claude, Material Contract Schedule.
metadata.subtitle: What a Skill Actually Is
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: did Claude learn contract law when it picked up the material-contract-schedule skill? Take the skill apart, show that it's a folder holding one SKILL.md read start-to-finish before the work begins, and land the trade-off — repeatability bought at the price of judgment.

beats.narration_text: Hear "Claude has a material-contract-schedule skill" and the natural read is a deal-review upgrade — like it studied M&A contracts on some training pass and came back knowing something it didn't before.
But nothing in the model's weights moved. Delete the skill's folder and Claude doesn't forget contract law — there was no new law to forget. It just loses one routine it was told to run.

Here's what's actually happening. A skill is one file. Material-contract-schedule is a folder holding a single SKILL.md — instructions, in plain English, for turning a stack of contracts into a structured disclosure schedule. Text you can open, read, and audit. Claude reads it before it starts.

The runtime is unglamorous: Claude reads that file top to bottom and executes it step by step, in the order it's written — no branching, no jumping ahead, unless the file itself says branch. Linear on purpose, so the same input goes through the same steps every run.

That makes a skill a specification, not a new power. They optimized for repeatability at the expense of judgment. The payoff: the same schedule structure every time — one row per contract, the same columns filled in. The cost: anything the file doesn't say, Claude is off the map.

So material-contract-schedule never taught Claude to judge a contract. What it guarantees is smaller and more valuable: every time the skill runs, Claude reads the same file and produces the same schedule structure. Same file, same routine, same shape — that's the whole trick.

beats.narration_text: The failure modes cut both ways. A schedule with every row filled in doesn't prove every contract was actually checked against the file's criteria — a cell can hold a confident-looking string with no fact behind it. And a schedule with gaps in it doesn't prove the skill is broken — it may just mean the file asked for something the contracts never said. The output shape doesn't tell you whether the work behind it was real.
A skill doesn't teach Claude what a material contract is — it's a file of ordered steps, read before the work starts, so the schedule comes out in the same shape every run.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. Pick one document you produce the same way every time — an incident report, a due-diligence memo, a customer summary. Ask the model to draft you a SKILL.md for it: the plain-English steps, in order, that anyone could follow to produce that document in the same shape every time. Then have the model walk you through what running the skill would look like, step by step, before it actually runs — so you can catch a bad step before it costs you. Go deeper: ask the same model to name three points in your SKILL.md where a step would fill itself in with something plausible-looking whether or not the work behind it was real.
